report.summary: During the requested investigation window (2026-10-26T10:17:36.257065+00:00 to 2026-10-26T13:17:36.257065+00:00), payment-service p95 latency rose 4.0x, from 0.24s to 0.94s. Logs show payment-service authorization failures and upstream timeouts calling fraud-api. These findings support investigating the fraud-api dependency path, but do not establish fraud-api's internal failure mechanism or prove it caused all of the latency increase.

likely_causes.title: Slow or unsuccessful calls to fraud-api
likely_causes.rationale: Timeouts calling fraud-api and authorization failures reporting the fraud check unavailable support the hypothesis that problems on the payment-service-to-fraud-api dependency path contributed to latency degradation. The evidence does not prove fraud-api's internal mechanism, that its latency rose first, or that all slow requests involved this dependency.

supporting_evidence.detail: payment-service WARN logs report upstream timeout calling fraud-api after 2000ms; 47 documents matched and 20 samples were retrieved.
11 payment-service ERROR documents report PaymentAuthorizationException: fraud check unavailable.
payment-service p95 latency rose 4.0x, from 0.24s to 0.94s; the metric finding is threshold-validated.

next_steps: Investigate fraud-api health and payment-service-to-fraud-api request latency, timeout rate, and distributed traces to verify whether the dependency path explains the latency increase.
Check request-rate metrics; no request-rate evidence was supplied, so increased traffic cannot be assessed.
Check deployment history and resource, queue, and saturation metrics; none were supplied to support or rule out deployment or resource-related hypotheses.
Treat the absence of matching fraud-api ERROR and timeout WARN documents as a lack of retrieved matching logs, not evidence that fraud-api was healthy.
Use timestamp-aligned metrics and traces to determine onset and correlation; the supplied aggregate metric trend and sampled log timestamps do not establish exact incident onset or causal ordering.
